1	# sw-MLPL Abstract Algebra, Visually
2	
3	Executable, **visual** demonstrations of abstract algebra — magmas,
4	semigroups, monoids, groups, and the structure-preserving maps between them —
5	written as standalone `.mlpl` scripts for the
6	[sw-MLPL](https://sw-ml-study.github.io/sw-mlpl/) interpreter.
7	
8	The premise is small and does a lot of work:
9	
10	> A finite binary operation on `n` elements **is** an `n x n` array.
11	
12	So building one is a single `table(f, elements, elements)`; every law is an
13	array predicate with no explicit loop; every counterexample is an index into
14	that array; and the array is directly renderable — which is why this is a
15	*visual* demo repository rather than a test suite.
16	
17	Two pictures do most of the teaching:
18	
19	- **The identity's cross.** When `e` is a two-sided identity, row `e` and
20	  column `e` reproduce the headings. Ring them and the definition explains
21	  itself.
22	- **The Latin square.** A group's table has every element exactly once in every
23	  row and column. Color by result and a group is recognizable at a glance; a
24	  mere monoid is not.
25	
26	Nothing here declares what a structure is. Each lesson hands `elements` and
27	`operation` to a classifier and reports what came back — magma, semigroup,
28	monoid, group, abelian group are **derived**, and a failed law names a witness
29	rather than returning `false`:
30	
31	```
32	  associativity counterexample:
33	    a = rock  b = paper  c = scissors
34	    (a*b)*c:  a*b = paper  ->  scissors
35	    a*(b*c):  b*c = scissors  ->  rock
36	```
37	
38	## Status
39	
40	Verified baseline: `mlpl-repl 0.20.0` from the adjacent
41	`../sw-mlpl/target/release` build, with mlplunit for conformance.

50	just demos     # run every lesson; artifacts land in out/
51	just tests     # mlplunit conformance suite
52	just check     # the full local gate
53	just render    # rebuild out/ and list what was written
54	```
55	
56	The interpreter is found at `../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl`, or wherever
57	`$MLPL` points. Nothing is installed and no stable binary is overwritten.
58	
59	## Layout
60	
61	```
62	lib/algebra.mlpl      laws, classification, counterexamples, homomorphisms
63	lib/render.mlpl       ASCII / SVG / JSON renderers
64	demos/NN-topic/*.mlpl one self-checking lesson per file

77	missing surface: sw-MLPL cannot concatenate two strings, cannot turn a number
78	into one, cannot measure or search one, and cannot build a string list. Since

80	These are specified for implementation — signatures, semantics, acceptance

48	- Classification is **derived, never declared.** No lesson says "this is a
49	  monoid"; each hands `elements` and `operation` to `u:classify` and reports
50	  what came back. That is the pedagogy and the acceptance test at once.
51	- Each lesson asserts its own invariants and ends in `ok(...)` / `err(...)`.
52	- Artifacts are an additional effect. Delete `out/` and every assertion still
53	  passes.
54	
55	## Lesson sequence
56	
57	The ladder is climbed one rung at a time, and the games are the hook rather
58	than the subject — they are gone by lesson 03.
59	
60	| # | Lesson | Concept | New visual | Status |
61	|---|---|---|---|---|
62	| 01 | `01-magmas/rock_paper_scissors` | Magma; closure; a law that fails | Colored Cayley table; ASCII grid | **done** |
63	| 02 | `02-rpsls/lizard_spock` | The same structure at n=5; function / table / graph as three views of one object | Dominance digraph in SVG, drawn on a circle | planned |
64	| 03 | `03-closure/escaping_the_set` | Closure by counterexample: an operation that leaves the set | Out-of-set cells struck out in grey | planned |
65	| 04 | `04-associativity/bracketing` | The `n^3` triple check; why the witness matters | The two bracketing cubes as stacked slices | planned |
66	| 05 | `05-semigroups/string_joins` | Associative but no identity | Latin-square-ness absent; no white cross | **needs blocker B3** |
67	| 06 | `06-monoids/identity_cross` | Identity discovered, not asserted; uniqueness | The white cross | planned |
68	| 07 | `07-inverses/undoing` | Inverses relative to the identity | Inverse pairs joined by chords over the table | planned |
69	| 08 | `08-groups/latin_square` | Groups; `Z_n` and the Klein four-group | The Latin square, side by side with a non-group | planned |
70	| 09 | `09-commutativity/symmetry` | Commutativity as a property, not a rung; `S_3` is not abelian | Reflection across the diagonal, animated in the viewer | planned |
71	| 10 | `10-enumeration/all_small_magmas` | Enumerate all `n^(n^2)` operations; classify them | Population bar chart of the ladder rungs | planned |
72	| 11 | `11-isomorphism/same_up_to_naming` | Relabeling; canonical forms; equivalence classes | Two tables shown becoming identical under a permutation | planned |
73	| 12 | `12-homomorphisms/structure_preserving` | `f(a*b) = f(a)*f(b)`; the bridge out of this repo | Two tables with arrows between them; violated cells flagged | planned |
74	
75	Lessons 13+ (rings, fields, two interacting operations) are a later saga, not
76	part of this plan.
77	
78	### Lesson 05 is currently blocked upstream
79	
80	Its natural subject is string concatenation — the canonical semigroup that is
81	not a monoid until you add `""`. sw-MLPL cannot concatenate strings
82	(`docs/mlpl-blockers.md`, B1) and cannot measure or search them (B3), so the
83	lesson is unwritable in its intended form today. Two ways forward, decided when
84	step 3 reaches it:
85	
86	- Wait for B1/B3 and write the lesson as intended. Preferred — it is the best
87	  example of the concept, and the lesson doubles as the adoption test for the
88	  new builtins.
89	- Substitute a non-string semigroup (`max` on a bounded set, or left
90	  projection) and note in the header that the natural example is blocked.
91	
92	Ship the substitute rather than stall the ladder, and replace it when B1/B3
93	land.
94	
95	### Lesson 10 is the serious array-programming workload
96	
97	For `n` elements there are `n^(n^2)` binary operations: 16 at `n=2`, 19,683 at
98	`n=3`. Enumerating and classifying all of them exercises generation,
99	combinatorics, higher-order predicates, filtering, grouping, and reduction —
100	the brief's point that "the mathematics generated the workload" rather than a
101	benchmark being invented for the language.
102	
103	The array formulation: an operation is a base-`n` numeral with `n^2` digits, so
104	all operations are one `[n^(n^2), n, n]` array produced by digit extraction over
105	`range(n^(n^2))`. Every law predicate then applies along the leading axis at
106	once. If the associativity cube cannot be lifted to a batch of tables without a
107	loop, that is a genuine finding for `docs/upstream-asks.md`, and the loop-based
108	version ships with the friction recorded.
109	
110	### Lesson 11 falls out of lesson 10
111	
112	19,683 tables at `n=3` collapse to far fewer once relabeling is quotiented out.
113	Canonical form = the lexicographically smallest table over all `n!`
114	permutations. `u:permute_table` already exists; the work is the quotient and
115	the count.
116	
117	## Visual layers, in the order they are built
118	
119	1. **ASCII first.** `disp()` renders any table in the terminal with no
120	   dependencies and no files. Every lesson has this. It is what survives when
121	   someone runs a demo over ssh.
122	2. **SVG second.** `lib/render.mlpl` emits its own SVG — headings, cell values,
123	   per-element color, and the identity cross. The built-in
124	   `svg(t, "heatmap")` colors cells but draws no headings, values, or
125	   highlights, which is most of the teaching (upstream ask #5).
126	3. **The interactive page last.** `viewer/cayley.html`: load a structure's
127	   JSON, edit a cell, watch the law verdicts recompute. This is where the
128	   brief's best idea lives — *"Make this magma associative"*, *"Turn this
129	   semigroup into a monoid"* as puzzles.
130	
131	The viewer re-implements the law checks in JavaScript, because a page cannot
132	call the interpreter. That duplication is deliberate and is kept honest:
133	`tests/test_viewer_conformance.mlpl` writes the fixture set the page's checker
134	must reproduce, and the MLPL result is authoritative. If they ever disagree,
135	the page is wrong.
136	
137	## Delivery sequence (saga steps)
138	
139	1. **Foundation** *(done)* — agentrail setup, harness, `lib/algebra.mlpl`,
140	   `lib/render.mlpl`, lesson 01, catalog, docs.

## Visualizing Data

The `svg(data, type)` built-in renders an array as an inline SVG
diagram. In the browser REPL the SVG is displayed directly below
the input; in the CLI REPL it prints a one-line summary and can
optionally be written to a file with `--svg-out <dir>`.

### Diagram types

```
# Scatter: Nx2 matrix of (x, y) points
svg([[0,0],[1,1],[2,4],[3,9],[4,16]], "scatter")

# Line: a vector becomes a polyline; Nx2 becomes connected (x,y) points
svg([1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6], "line")

# Bar: one bar per element of a vector
svg([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6], "bar")

# Heatmap: MxN matrix as a colored grid (viridis ramp)
svg(reshape(iota(25), [5, 5]), "heatmap")
```

### Loss curve walkthrough

=== include in browser ===

- The path is one literal, relative path -- never computed,
  absolute, or conditional. `include` is only legal at the top
  level of a source file (not inside blocks or functions), and
  only in script mode: the browser session, connect mode, and
  interactive prompt answer it with a precise error instead.
- Included definitions (`u:` functions, bindings) enter the
  program at the include site, in source order.
- Resolution is sandboxed. `mlpl-repl --source-dir DIR -f
  script.mlpl` roots all includes under DIR; without the flag
  the root is the script's own directory. Escaping the root
